title: Per-request Kernel Priority and KV-rank Scheduling Notes
content:
Context:

This is a sketchy working doc collecting experiments and design ideas around per-request kernel prioritization and ranking of KV entries for paged-KV systems. The motivation: high-SLO interactive requests should not suffer large tail latency because of noisy background workload (batching, large prompts, embeddings jobs). Existing request-level routing only looks at model variant and region; we need finer-grained scheduling inside the GPU runtime.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Establish a cheap, low-jitter mechanism to prefer short/interactive requests at kernel launch time (not just at queueing).
- Combine kernel-priority with paged-KV rank to decide which KV pages to prefetch and which to evict when memory pressure hits.
- Make FlashAttention/fused-op launches aware of priority lanes so that critical short requests get smaller microbatches and faster kernel variants.
- Avoid starvation of lower-priority work while preserving latency SLOs.

Problem statement / Constraints:
- We run a mixed workload: chat (short, low-token requests), long-completion pipelines (high token count), and background offline batches.
- Paged-KV means not all KV fits on GPU; fetching a page is O(rtt) and can block token generation if not prefetched.
- FlashAttention choices: different kernel shapes and tilings are efficient at different seq lengths and batch sizes. Launching the wrong kernel (e.g., flash kernel optimized for long sequences) for a short interactive request can inflate latency by 2-3x.
- Kernel launch overhead and GPU stream contention matter: we cannot simply serialize everything on a single high-priority stream.

High-level sketch (priority + KV-rank):
1) Each incoming request is assigned a priority lane: P0 (interactive/hot), P1 (standard), P2 (background/low). Priority assignment comes from frontdoor config (API route metadata + SLA tier).
2) At request admission time we compute a lightweight KV-rank vector: list of KV pages/segments predicted to be needed in next N tokens, ranked by probability or recency. This uses model prompt analysis + last-token context heuristics (cheap).
3) The scheduler maintains per-lane token budgets and a per-lane prefetch budget: how many concurrent page fetches allowed. P0 gets prefetch budget spike when latency SLO at risk.
4) Kernel variants (FlashOptSmall, FlashOptLarge, FusedSmall, FusedLarge) are annotated with preferred lane masks and expected latency/cost profiles. Launch mechanism picks variant based on lane and dynamic occupancy estimate.

Runtime components to implement (notes):
- Request descriptor (small, ~64 bytes) attached to each work item: {lane, estimated_tokens, kv_rank_topk (IDs), weight}. Keep representation compact for queueing.
- Lane-aware stream pools: Have 2-3 CUDA stream pools per GPU tagged by lane. High-priority kernels go to P0 streams with strict preemption window semantics (soft preemption: small kernels launched immediately on P0 stream, long kernels get split or kicked to P1).
- Kernel splitter: For long requests that happen to be P0 (rare), split token generation into smaller micro-batches so any single kernel call stays under a latency budget. This interacts with KV cache locality and batching efficiency.
- Prefetch controller: Given kv_rank_topk from admission, prefetch controller issues DMA/page fetch ops with lane-weighted concurrency. It exposes backpressure tokens to the request descriptor so the token-generation path knows whether needed pages are hot.

KV-rank heuristics (sketch):
- Basic: recency-based + prompt sliding window. For chat this means recent messages' KV pages get high rank.
- Predictive: run a cheap ngram/trimmed LM predictor on prompt to estimate token-level attention span (i.e., which layers/positions likely to be referenced) => map to pages.
- Weighting: weight pages by rank * expected future tokens. P0 requests get multiplicative boost to top-k scores to improve prefetch hit.

Prefetch backpressure and credit model:
- Each GPU tracks page fetch bandwidth and pending latencies. When headroom low, controller reduces background P2 prefetch concurrency first, then P1, preserving P0.
- Credits: on admission a request gets X prefetch credits based on lane. Each page fetch consumes 1 credit. When credits exhausted, subsequent needed pages are queued with lower priority.
- Soft degrade: if critical pages missing at generation time, fall back to local software-attention path that can compute attention without page (slower but non-blocking), or reduce kv lookback window (graceful quality vs latency tradeoff).

FlashAttention + fused ops considerations:
- Kernel selection: maintain a small LUT mapping (seq_len_bucket, batch_size_bucket, lane) -> kernel_variant. LUT updated offline from microbench results and warmed up in runtime.
- For P0 we bias toward low-latency kernel variant even if slightly more FLOPs. For P2 bias toward highest throughput/lowest-cost variant.
- Fused ops (e.g., attention + feedforward fusion): fusion increases per-kernel latency but reduces total scheduling overhead. For small seq/batch (P0) fused kernels might be worse; thus prefer unfused smaller kernels for P0. Need per-variant occupancy breakpoints.

Memory/eviction policy interplay with KV-rank:
- Eviction should be rank-aware and lane-aware. Hot pages with high aggregate rank across active P0 requests get protection tokens.
- Implement a two-tier eviction: 1) fast-pass eviction candidate selection using bloom filter + usage counters, 2) slow-pass exact LRU-like eviction for pages frequently contested.
- Consider probationary promotion: when a P0 prefetch brings in a page, mark it protected for T ms; if not used within T, drop protection. Tunables: T ~ 100-500ms.

Microbench plan (quick experiments to run):
1) Kernel LUT generation: run microbench across seq=[8,16,32,64,128,256], batch=[1,2,4,8,16], measure latency for Flash small/large/fused/unfused. Do this under 3 occupancy levels (10%, 50%, 90%). Output LUT with percentiles.
2) Prefetch credit simulation: synthetic workload mix {P0:40%, P1:40%, P2:20%} with realistic token lengths and page access patterns. Simulate credit allocation and measure P0 tail latency.
3) Split vs unsplit: For long P0 requests (>128 tokens) experimentally measure splitting into 8-token kernel windows vs single kernel. Metrics: tail latency, overall GPU utilization, KV hit-rate.
4) Eviction policies: compare naive LRU, rank-weighted eviction, protected pages with T=200ms. Metric: P0 miss-rate and overall page churn.

Preliminary observations (from quick local probe on A100 devbox):
- Flash kernel variants show 1.8-2.4x latency divergence across seq-length buckets for batch=1.
- Small fused kernels add ~30-60us overhead per launch but reduce total copies; for batch=1+seq<=32 they degrade latency vs unfused.
- Prefetch concurrency > 8 on our NIC -> causes jitter; credit mechanism necessary.

Open questions and risks:
- Starvation safety: how to prevent adversarial streams that tag everything P0? Need token-budget enforcement at the API ingress.
- Complexity vs benefit: introducing lane-aware streams, prefetch credits, and kernel LUT increases runtime complexity; need a fallback simpler policy.
- Accuracy of KV-rank predictor: if predictor poor, prefetch wasted and evictions harmful. Consider adding an online learning loop to adjust weights.
- Portability: design must degrade gracefully on multicard setups and without NVLink. Page fetch semantics differ across infra.

Action items / TODOs:
- [ ] Run full microbench grid and populate kernel LUT (owner: Eric). Target: 2024-10-09.
- [ ] Prototype prefetch credit controller in runtime (owner: Ravi). Minimal API: grant_credits(request_id, k).
- [ ] Implement request descriptor attachable to queue items (owner: Ava). Keep serialized size <128B.
- [ ] Write simulation harness for eviction policies (owner: Lena).
- [ ] Design a simple safe mode: single global lane policy that preserves correctness when config disabled.

Notes-to-self:
- Keep initial rollout conservative: enable lane-aware scheduling behind feature flag per-customer.
- Add observability: token-level latency histogram per lane, per-kernel variant percentiles, page-prefetch hit/miss rates by lane.

References and scribbles:
- See GH PR linked above for proto types.
- Related idea: credit-based batching (where batch slots are assigned per lane). Might be combined with this work.

Unresolved: exact prefetch credit numbers, eviction protection TTL, kernel LUT bucket boundaries. Need data.

End of doc.
